540.title: He made Himself
540.hook: He created Himself, then the Name, then the world, and sat watching it with delight (Asa di Var 1, ang 463)
540.howItsDone: The first pauri of Asa di Var, sung each morning in gurdwaras, describes God as self-made, taking on the Name, making the world, and sitting within it to watch with delight.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a hundred moons, and your line: the guru is the light. Did you sit a breath in the dark last night? Two saloks of thanks and light are behind us. Today we reach the first pauri, the first rung of the ballad. Day five hundred forty.
screen: `A HUNDRED MOONS — THE GURU IS THE LIGHT.`

segments.voice: A potter finishes a bowl, sets it on the shelf, and steps back. A gardener stands at the edge of a bed she planted in spring, now full of tomatoes. A father watches his daughter take her first wobbly steps across the kitchen. There's a particular look on a maker's face in that moment, half pride and half wonder, as if they can't quite believe it's real. The first pauri of Asa di Var says God has that look too.
screen: `A POTTER STEPS BACK.` → `A GARDEN FULL OF TOMATOES.` → `THE LOOK ON A MAKER'S FACE.`

segments.voice: The first pauri begins, in paraphrase: He Himself fashioned Himself, and Himself took on the Name. Second, He made the creation, and seated within it, He watches it with delight. Then it turns to praise: You are the Giver and the Maker; pleased, You give and bless. You know everyone; You give life and can take it back with a word. Take the order slowly. First, aapeenai aap saajio: He made Himself. Nobody made God. God is self-existent, the same idea Sikhs recite every day in the Mool Mantar as saibhang, self-existent. Second, the Name: God takes on naau, the Name, which in Gurbani means God made known, God expressed. And only then, the world, kudrat, the creation. Then the lovely part: kar aasan, having taken a seat, ditho chaau, He watched with delight. Aasan is a seat, the cushion or mat you sit on. God doesn't make the world and leave, like a builder handing over keys. God sits down inside it. And chaau is delight, eagerness, the joy of a festival or a wedding. So the God of this first pauri isn't a distant engineer, or a grim judge. It's a maker who sits down in the middle of the work and enjoys it. That says something about the world, too. If its Maker watches it with delight, then it's worth delighting in: tomatoes, first steps, the bowl on the shelf. Before Asa di Var gets sharp about pride and pretending, as it will, it sets this down first: a world made with joy.
screen: `FIRST: HE MADE HIMSELF.` · `THEN THE NAME, THEN THE WORLD.` · `AASAN: HE SITS DOWN INSIDE IT.` · `CHAAU: DELIGHT, LIKE A FESTIVAL.` · then, large: `WATCHING WITH DELIGHT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: watch something you made. Find it, or picture it: a meal you cooked, a garden, a drawing, a shelf you built, a letter, a child you raised, a friendship you tended. Sit with it the way the pauri says God sits with creation. Not judging the flaws; just watching, with delight. Let the corners of your mouth lift if they want to. If you pray, you can rest in Waheguru, the Maker who watches with delight. The bell holds the time.
He made Himself. Asa di Var's first pauri: God made Himself, then the Name, then the world, and took a seat within it, watching with delight.
Your line: watching with delight. Today, when you finish any small task, pause one breath and look at it with delight, before rushing on. Day five hundred forty.

541.title: The salok of wonder
541.hook: wonder is the sound, wonder the scripture, wonder the creatures, wonder the colors (Asa di Var, ang 463)
541.howItsDone: Asa di Var's salok of wonder, sung each morning in gurdwaras, repeats vismaad line after line, and Sikhs hear the same awe in waah, the opening of Waheguru.

segments.voice: Yesterday, he made himself, and your line: watching with delight. Did you pause to enjoy one finished task? The Maker sat down inside creation, delighted. Today Guru Nanak looks at that same creation and can't stop saying one word. Day five hundred forty-one.

Watch a toddler meet a dog for the first time. The eyes go wide. The mouth opens. Sometimes there's a sound, a long whoa, and sometimes just silence, a whole small body gone still with astonishment. Then the child points, and looks at you, as if to say: are you seeing this? Most adults lost that look somewhere along the way. We've seen dogs. We've seen rain. We've seen the moon. Guru Nanak, in Asa di Var, writes a salok that sounds like that toddler's whoa, repeated over and over.
screen: `A TODDLER MEETS A DOG.` → `EYES WIDE, A LONG WHOA.` → `ARE YOU SEEING THIS?`

segments.voice: The salok begins almost every phrase with one word: vismaad. Wonder, awe, astonishment. In paraphrase, it runs like this. Wonder is the sound, wonder is the sacred knowledge. Wonder are the living beings, wonder their many kinds. Wonder are the forms, wonder the colors. Wonder, creatures wandering about unclothed. Wonder is the wind, wonder the water, wonder the fire that plays its marvels. Wonder the earth, wonder the sources of life. Wonder, union; wonder, parting. Wonder, hunger; wonder, being fed. Wonder near, wonder far. It keeps going, line after line, like a drumbeat. Notice what Guru Nanak puts on the list. Not only lovely things. Parting is there, and hunger, and the wilderness alongside the path. Vismaad isn't a sunset filter laid over the hard parts of life. It's astonishment at all of it, the whole strange, enormous fact that anything exists at all. And then the ending, in paraphrase: seeing these marvels, I am struck with wonder. Nanak says, to understand this comes by perfect good fortune. In Sikh teaching, vismaad isn't just a feeling. It's a spiritual state: the place where cleverness runs out and only awe is left. Many Sikhs hear the same awe in the name they use for God, Waheguru, which opens with waah, the Punjabi cry of wonder. The toddler's whoa, in other words, is not so far from prayer. Today's salok gives grown-ups permission to point at the world and say: are you seeing this?
screen: `VISMAAD: WONDER, AWE.` · `SOUND, BEINGS, COLORS, WIND, FIRE.` · `HUNGER AND PARTING ARE ON THE LIST.` · `WAAH: THE CRY IN WAHEGURU.` · then, large: `WONDER, WONDER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find three wonders outside. If you can, step outside or to a window. If not, picture the last time you were outdoors. Look slowly until something catches you: the shape of a cloud, a weed in a crack, the sound of a bird or a distant train. That's one. Stay with it, and let it be astonishing. Then find a second, and a third. Don't hurry. If you pray, you can whisper Waheguru at each one. The bell holds the time.
Vismaad. Wonder and awe; Guru Nanak's salok in Asa di Var sees vismaad in sound, beings, colors, wind, water, hunger and parting, near and far.
Your line: wonder, wonder. Today, point out one wonder to someone else, a child, a friend, a coworker, and ask: are you seeing this? Day five hundred forty-one.

542.title: All is His power
542.hook: by His power we see and hear, by His power fear and joy (Asa di Var, ang 464)
542.howItsDone: Sikhs hear this salok when Asa di Var is sung in the gurdwara at dawn, and the word kudrat is common in everyday Punjabi for nature and the created world.

segments.voice: Yesterday, vismaad, the salok of wonder, and your line: wonder, wonder. Did you find your three wonders outside? Today the very next salok takes that wonder and gives it a name. Day five hundred forty-two.

Hold your hand up to a window and look at it. The skin, the lines across the palm, the faint pulse at the wrist. You didn't design any of it. You didn't decide to have eyes that could see it, or a brain that could wonder about it. Yesterday Guru Nanak stood in front of creation and could only say wonder. Today, in the salok right after, he does something more. He looks at the same world, item by item, and names the force running through every piece. One word, said again and again, like a drumbeat: kudrat.
screen: `LOOK AT YOUR OWN HAND.` → `YOU DIDN'T DESIGN ANY OF IT.` → `ONE WORD, LIKE A DRUMBEAT.`

segments.voice: Kudrat came into Punjabi from Arabic and Persian. It means power, the power to make and to do, and in everyday Punjabi it also came to mean nature, the created world itself. Both meanings hum in this salok, on ang 464. Guru Nanak begins with the senses. By your power we see, by your power we hear. By your power there is fear, and there is joy, the very core of happiness. Then the list widens. Your power is in the worlds below and the skies above, in every form. Your power is in the scriptures, he says, naming the Vedas and Puranas and the Semitic books alike. It's in eating and drinking and getting dressed. It's in love. It's in every species and kind and color, in the air and water and fire, in the dust of the earth. And then the line that surprises people. Your power is in good deeds, and your power is in bad ones. Honor and pride, too. Guru Nanak doesn't keep a clean list of only pleasant things. Everything that happens, happens inside this one power. The salok ends by turning to the One directly: all is your kudrat, and you are kaadir, the powerful Creator. Kaadir and kudrat share a root, so it sounds like a signature: the power and the Powerful belong together. And the last line says Nanak sees the One at work within the hukam, the divine order, utterly alone and beyond all. So the point isn't fear of a strong God. It's attention. If power is in the seeing, then your next glance is already part of it. If it's in the eating, then lunch is part of it. A Sikh walking through an ordinary day, the salok suggests, never leaves the creation's workshop.
screen: `KUDRAT: POWER, AND NATURE.` · `IN SEEING, HEARING, FEAR AND JOY.` · `IN GOOD DEEDS AND IN BAD.` · `KUDRAT AND KAADIR: ONE ROOT.` · then, large: `ALL IS YOUR POWER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice power in a leaf. If you can, step outside or find a plant indoors. If not, picture one clearly. Look at a single leaf. Follow one vein from the stem to the edge. Think of what is happening inside it right now, without anyone's help: light becoming food, water rising from the roots. Let your breath slow while you watch. Then look at your own hand again, and notice the same quiet work going on there. If you pray, you can say Waheguru once, softly. The bell holds the time.
Kudrat. Power, and the creation that power makes. In Guru Nanak's salok, it runs through seeing, hearing, eating, loving, and every color on earth.
Your line: his power. Today, at three ordinary moments, a glass of water, a song you hear, a stranger's laugh, say the word kudrat under your breath. Day five hundred forty-two.

543.title: In awe the wind blows
543.hook: in awe the wind blows and rivers run; only the Formless is without fear (Asa di Var, ang 464)
543.howItsDone: Sikhs hear this salok of awe in the dawn singing of Asa di Var, and many know its refrain, bhai vich, in awe, from long listening in the gurdwara.

segments.voice: Yesterday, kudrat, power and nature in one word, and your line: his power. Which ordinary moment did you name with it? Today a salok a little further on shows the whole creation moving in awe. Day five hundred forty-three.

Every morning the sun comes up within a few minutes of when the tables say it will. Tides arrive on schedule. Rivers that have run downhill for thousands of years are still running downhill today. Nobody stands at the top of the mountain and tells the water where to go. Scientists call these patterns laws. Guru Nanak, looking at the same faithful river and the same punctual sun, reached for a word you might not expect. Not law. Not order. Bhau. Fear, or awe. And in one long salok he hears the entire universe living inside it.
screen: `THE SUN, ON SCHEDULE.` → `RIVERS STILL RUN DOWNHILL.` → `GURU NANAK'S WORD: BHAU.`

segments.voice: Bhau is the Punjabi word at the center of this salok on ang 464, and it's hard to put into English. It can mean fear. But in Gurbani it often means something closer to reverence: the trembling respect you feel standing at the edge of a canyon. Listen to how the salok builds. Bhai vich, in awe, the wind blows, always. In awe a hundred thousand rivers flow. In awe fire does its work. In awe the earth carries its load. In awe the clouds move, the sun and the moon travel their endless miles. In awe stand the wise and the powerful, the warriors and the heroes, and in awe the crowds of people come and go. Notice the pictures. Wind that never takes a day off. Rivers that never refuse. Fire that keeps burning as if under orders. Guru Nanak is describing faithfulness. Everything in creation keeps its place and does its job, because it moves within the One's hukam, the divine order. Bhau, here, is what that looks like from the inside. Then comes the turn. Awe, the salok says, is written on every forehead. All of it. Sun, river, king, saint. Only one is without fear: the Formless, the One who is true. Tomorrow we stay with that line. For today, one thing. In Sikh teaching, this awe isn't meant to make a person small and frightened. Elsewhere in Gurbani, bhau and bhaau, awe and love, often travel together, and Sikhs describe the right kind of awe as what keeps love honest. The wind doesn't blow out of terror. It blows because it knows where it belongs.
screen: `BHAU: FEAR, OR AWE.` · `WIND, RIVERS, FIRE, EARTH, SUN.` · `EVERYTHING KEEPS ITS PLACE.` · `ONLY THE FORMLESS IS WITHOUT FEAR.` · then, large: `IN AWE THE WIND BLOWS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: feel the wind. If you can, open a window or step outside for a minute. If the air is still, feel your own breath instead, the small wind you carry everywhere. Notice where it touches you: your face, your hands, the inside of your nose. Notice that it moves without being asked. Then let a little of the salok's awe settle in: this air has been moving faithfully since long before you, and will move long after. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on the out-breath. The bell holds the time.
In awe the wind blows. Guru Nanak's picture of a faithful creation: wind, rivers, fire, earth, sun and moon, all moving within the One's order.
screen: `IN AWE THE WIND BLOWS — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: everything in awe. Today, watch one thing that keeps its rhythm without being told: a clock, a tide chart, your own heartbeat. Let it remind you of the wind. Day five hundred forty-three.

544.title: The fearless Formless
544.hook: Nanak says the Formless alone is fearless; all else is dust by comparison (Asa di Var, ang 464)
544.howItsDone: Sikhs meet the word nirbhau every day in the Mool Mantar, and hear this salok on the fearless Formless when Asa di Var is sung at dawn.

segments.voice: Yesterday, in awe the wind blows, and your line: everything in awe. Wind, rivers, sun, kings, all of it moving within the order. And one alone without fear. Today we stand with that one line. Day five hundred forty-four.

If you've been on this path since the first year, you already know the word. It sits in the Mool Mantar, the opening lines of the Guru Granth Sahib, right after the Creator and before without hate: nirbhau. Without fear. You may have said it a hundred times. Yesterday's salok ended on it, after a whole universe of trembling: only the Formless is without fear. And today's salok, the next one in the var, starts there and refuses to move on quickly. Nanak, it says. The Formless is fearless. And then it looks at everything else people admire.
screen: `NIRBHAU, FROM THE MOOL MANTAR.` → `A UNIVERSE OF TREMBLING.` → `ONLY ONE WITHOUT FEAR.`

segments.voice: Two words carry this salok on ang 464. Nirbhau: nir, without, and bhau, the fear and awe we met yesterday. And nirankar: nir again, without, and akar, form or shape. The Formless. Put them together and you have Guru Nanak's answer to a very human question: is there anything that isn't afraid? Everything with a form, he says, lives with fear. Forms can break. Forms can be lost. The salok goes on to list what people admire and tell stories about, and sets each beside the Formless. So many celebrated figures, it says, are like dust. So many tales are told and retold, so many learned arguments made. People dance and sing for a crowd. Others wear earrings and necklaces worth a fortune, and the bodies that wear them, the salok says plainly, turn to ash. Then it makes a turn worth noticing. Real wisdom, it says, isn't found through talk. Speaking of the One is as hard as iron. It comes by grace; cleverness and display only wear a person out. Here's why this matters on a Tuesday. Most of our fears are about forms: a body getting sick, a job disappearing, a reputation cracking, a person leaving. The salok doesn't tell anyone those fears are silly. Forms really do pass. What it offers is a place to stand. If only the Formless is fearless, then the way through fear, in Sikh teaching, isn't to become hard and fearless yourself. It's to stay close to the One who is. Sikhs often say it in a short phrase: the one who fears the One fears nothing else.
screen: `NIR-BHAU: WITHOUT FEAR.` · `NIR-AKAR: WITHOUT FORM.` · `EVERY FORM CAN BREAK.` · `WISDOM COMES BY GRACE, NOT TALK.` · then, large: `ONLY THE FORMLESS IS FEARLESS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let one fear shrink. Sit comfortably and breathe out slowly. Let one fear come to mind, a real one, not the biggest. Notice what form it's attached to: your health, your money, your work, a person. Picture it the size it feels right now. Then, in your mind, set it beside the whole sky, the wind, the rivers from yesterday, everything moving in its order. Watch it take its true size. You don't have to make it disappear. If you pray, you can say nirbhau, nirankar, quietly. The bell holds the time.
The fearless Formless. Nirbhau, without fear, and nirankar, without form: the One beside whom every form, however admired, is dust.
Your line: only he is fearless. Today, when a worry flares, name the form it's clinging to, and say the line once. Day five hundred forty-four.

545.title: The contented served
545.hook: those who served in contentment and meditated on truth were accepted (Asa di Var, ang 466)
545.howItsDone: Sikhs practice seva, selfless service, in the gurdwara kitchen, cleaning, and serving the community, and this pauri of Asa di Var describes the contented spirit behind it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the fearless Formless, and your line: only he is fearless. Did a worry shrink when you named its form? Today, a pauri about the people who lived close to that One. Day five hundred forty-five.

Visit a big gurdwara kitchen early in the morning and watch the people working there. Someone is stirring a pot of dal the size of a bathtub. Someone is rolling rotis at a speed that looks impossible. An old man is stacking steel plates. Nobody is checking a clock to see when the shift ends, and nobody is waiting for thanks. If you ask one of them why they're there, they might just shrug and hand you a ball of dough. Guru Nanak described people like this in a single pauri, and the pauri turns on one word.
screen: `A GURDWARA KITCHEN AT DAWN.` → `NOBODY WAITING FOR THANKS.` → `GURU NANAK'S ONE WORD.`

segments.voice: The pauri is on ang 466, and it opens like this, in paraphrase: those who served were the contented ones, the ones who meditated on truth and nothing but truth. The word is santokh. Contentment. You've met it before on this path: Japji calls contentment one of the earrings of the true yogi. Here, it's what makes service real. Then the pauri describes these people. They did not set their foot on the path of wrong. They did good and lived by dharam, by righteousness. They broke the world's chains, and they ate and drank only a little. And then the pauri turns to the One: you are the great giver, always giving more. By greatness, the Great One is found. So why contentment, of all things? Think about what discontent does to service. If you serve hoping to be noticed, every unnoticed hour stings. If you serve to get something back, you're keeping score. If you serve while wishing you were somewhere else, the work feels heavy and so do you. Contentment takes all of that out. It doesn't mean doing nothing or wanting nothing for the world. It means being at peace with your own share while you work for others. Eating a little, the pauri says, is part of the picture: not needing much leaves room for giving. In Sikh life, seva, selfless service, is everywhere: in the langar, in cleaning shoes, in sweeping the floor. This pauri gives seva its inner side. The hands serve. The heart is content. And the pauri says the ones who served that way were accepted.
screen: `SANTOKH: CONTENTMENT.` · `THEY DID GOOD AND ATE LITTLE.` · `DISCONTENT KEEPS SCORE.` · `HANDS SERVE, HEART CONTENT.` · then, large: `THE CONTENTED SERVED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: serve contentedly. Sit for a moment and pick one small service you can do in the next hour: washing a few dishes, refilling someone's water, tidying a shared space. Before you do it, breathe out slowly and let go of any wish to be noticed. Picture yourself doing it fully, and finishing, and walking away without needing anyone to see. Feel what that's like in your chest. If you pray, you can say Waheguru. When the bell ends, go and do it. The bell holds the time.
The contented served. Guru Nanak's picture of true servants: content with little, rooted in truth, doing good without keeping score.
Your line: contented service. Today, do one helpful thing and tell no one about it, not even later tonight. Day five hundred forty-five.

546.title: What ego is
546.hook: this is ego: in ego we act, in ego we come and go; and the cure is within (Asa di Var M2, ang 466)
546.howItsDone: Sikhs hear Guru Angad's salok on haumai in the dawn singing of Asa di Var, and Sikh teaching treats overcoming ego through the Guru's word as central to the spiritual life.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the contented served, and your line: contented service. Did your helpful thing stay a secret? It's the end of a week, too: He made Himself, wonder, kudrat, the wind in awe, the fearless Formless, contented servants. Today, what gets in the way of all of it. Day five hundred forty-six.
screen: `CONTENTED SERVICE.` · `A WEEK: WONDER, POWER, AWE, SERVICE.`

segments.voice: Someone gives you a compliment, and for a second your chest swells. Someone else cuts in front of you in line, and for a second your face goes hot. Someone corrects you in a meeting, and you spend the whole afternoon replaying it. Three different feelings, one common center: me. Guru Angad, the second Guru, wrote a salok that sits on the same page of the Asa di Var as the pauri of the contented servants. It reads almost like a doctor's notes. Here's the illness, he says. Here's what it does. Here's where it comes from. And here, surprisingly, is where the medicine is kept.
screen: `PRAISE, INSULT, CORRECTION.` → `ONE CENTER: ME.` → `A DOCTOR'S NOTES FROM GURU ANGAD.`

segments.voice: The word is haumai. Hau means I, and mai is often read as me or mine, so haumai is something like I-me-ness: the self that keeps putting itself at the center. The salok, marked mahala 2 for Guru Angad, is on ang 466. In paraphrase: this is the nature of haumai. In haumai people do their deeds. This is haumai's bondage: again and again it brings people back into birth. Then Guru Angad asks two questions out loud. Where does haumai come from? And by what discipline does it leave? His answer to the first is honest and a little startling: haumai exists by the hukam, the divine order. It's part of how humans are made. People wander, he says, according to what they've done before. So ego isn't treated as a shameful secret or a monster. It's a condition. And then the line that gives today its carry. Haumai is a deep, chronic illness. But the medicine, he says, is also within it. Daaroo bhee is maahi. The cure is in the same place as the disease. How? If the One gives grace, Guru Angad says, a person begins to live by the Guru's word, the shabad. And then, Nanak says, listen, people: by this discipline the pain goes. Think about what that means. The same I that grabs credit can also notice that it's grabbing. The same I that replays an insult can choose to stop. Sikh teaching doesn't ask people to destroy the self. It asks them to turn it, through the shabad, from the center of everything toward the One.
screen: `HAUMAI: I-ME-NESS.` · `WHERE DOES IT COME FROM?` · `A CHRONIC ILLNESS.` · `THE MEDICINE IS WITHIN.` · then, large: `EGO, AND ITS CURE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: watch one ego move. Sit and breathe slowly. Think back over the last day and find one small moment where the I jumped to the center: a flash of pride, a sting, a need to be right. Don't judge it. Just watch it play again, like a short video. Notice where you felt it in your body. Then notice who's watching. That noticing is the medicine Guru Angad talks about, already at work. If you pray, you can say Waheguru, and let the moment go. The bell holds the time.
What ego is. Haumai, I-me-ness, in Guru Angad's words: a chronic illness that keeps the self at the center, with its medicine found within.
Your line: ego, and its cure. Today, when you catch your I jumping to the center, smile at it once instead of following it. Day five hundred forty-six.
